It's polling day in the US midterms, with millions of Americans voting to decide who will control Congress for the final two years of Donald Trump's presidency

What's up for election? See our basic explainer here

Trump's Republican Party currently controls the two chambers - the House of Representatives and the Senate - but Democrats are hoping to flip enough seats to win a majority in both

If they control Congress, Democrats would be better placed to block Trump's plans, and could also launch investigations into the president and his team

This could include an attempt to impeach Trump, writes our North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher

Donald Trump spoke at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool yesterday

US President Donald Trump has been busy online today, repeatedly posting endorsements on his social media site Truth Social.

He is also still thinking about his Reflecting Pool renovation project, which was at the centre of his speech in Washington yesterday - his last public remarks before today's midterms.

Twice in the last hour or so, Trump has posted about the pool, which has been the subject of a controversial renovation.

In one post, he criticised the Daily Mail for its coverage of his final midterm event yesterday, which he termed a \"news conference\" rather than a \"speech\".

In a second post, he accused California Democratic Representative Ted Liu of spreading \"malicious, false and defamatory statements\" that Trump wanted to rename the pool after himself.

The pool, and a number of other large-scale renovation and construction sites in Washington, are a topic that is important to President Trump - he mentions them regularly.

His focus on the pool yesterday raised eyebrows among observers who wondered what, if any, electoral benefit such remarks would have when polls show that many Americans are primarily concerned with the US economy.

Trump still posting about Reflecting Pool on voting day

Protesters in January demonstrate against

Raids and detentions have brought one of the country's top political issues - immigration - right to the neighbourhoods and doorsteps of many Latino families in Florida.

For many, actions taken by the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency (ICE) are personal, affecting relatives, friends and entire communities.

The impact is being felt even among groups who have traditionally enjoyed more favourable treatment under US immigration law, including Cuban Americans, many of whom supported president Trump in the 2024 election.

Latino families in the state have also been affected, both directly and indirectly, by the Trump administration's restrictions on asylum and ending of temporary deportation protections for roughly one million migrants who entered the US during the Biden administration.

Now, the big question is: Will growing frustration with Trump translate into votes for Democrats and how many Latino voters, particularly Cuban and Venezuelan Americans in Florida, will stick with Republicans.

While some may oppose Trump's immigration policies, others may be reluctant to weaken his political position, fearing he would have a harder time delivering on promises to \"take care of Cuba\" or \"make Venezuela great again\".

Will Florida's Latinos stick with Trump and Republicans despite ICE raids?

The priorities of the roughly 39 million Hispanic Americans eligible to vote in the US vary widely depending on their background, age and where they live. Yet many of their concerns mirror those of the wider electorate.

The economy, inflation and the cost of living are their top concerns, in a country where the average price of petrol has reached $4.17 (£3) a gallon, a record for an election day.

In 2024, Donald Trump made significant gains among Hispanic voters, winning nearly half of their votes - a notable shift from previous elections. Those gains were particularly strong among Latino men and in communities across South Texas and Florida.

Two years on, polls suggest some of that support has eroded.

Trump's approval rating among Latino voters has fallen, and a growing number of those who backed him in 2024 are now expressing disappointment with his administration. According to the Pew Research Center, his approval rating among Latinos who voted for him two years ago has dropped from 93% to 57%.

Beyond the economy, many Latinos are also frustrated with his hard-line immigration policies. While there is broad support among voters for tighter border controls, many believe the administration has gone too far with its deportations.

After shifting toward Trump two years ago, many Hispanic Americans are moving away

Trump courted supporters in Lubbock during the midterm campaign trail

Two years ago, Trump won Lubbock, Texas, with 70% of the vote. It’s about as conservative as it gets.

The dusty plains city hosted duelling campaign rallies last week, with President Trump and Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico separated by just a few miles.

Thousands lined the roads around the airport to watch Air Force One land, and more gathered at a rally for Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton.

What I heard from Talarico’s supporters was a mixture of hope and dread.

The hope was that their candidate would be the first Democrat in more than three decades to win a state-wide race in Texas. The dread was that this would be just the latest example of Democratic optimism dashed.

Republican strategists I spoke with were clear-eyed about the challenge.

Perhaps their greatest concern is that if Democrats break through, Democratic efforts will turn to Texas ahead of the 2028 presidential election, forcing Republicans to defend what was safe terrain just a few years ago.
